summary: A 1977 Telnet option for byte macros, which let one side send a short code that stands for a longer string of characters. It was replaced by RFC 735.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 729 describes a Telnet option for replacing a longer string with one byte. Once the other side accepts the mapping, it expands that byte when received.

questions: what is the telnet byte macro option
how does a telnet byte macro work
subtitle: A Telnet option replaces a longer expansion string with a single data byte.

tldr.problem: Telnet option subcommands can take at least five characters on the wire, creating overhead when control markers are sent often in small blocks.
tldr.mechanism: After negotiating BM, a sender defines a data byte to stand for an expansion string. The receiver treats that byte as if the expansion string had arrived.
tldr.outcome: RFC 729 presents BM as a simple compression technique for reducing control overhead. It was obsoleted by RFC 735.

today: RFC 729 was obsoleted by RFC 735. It documents a Telnet byte-macro option intended to reduce subcommand overhead.

sections.title: Reducing Subcommand Overhead
sections.content: The RFC says Telnet subcommands require a minimum of five characters to transmit. If a block-oriented data stream needs a separator after every small block, control information can take up much of the traffic. The BM option is intended to reduce that overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Short blocks can require many control characters between them. BM proposes using a compact byte for a longer string.

sections.title: Negotiating Byte Macros
sections.content: The BM option is enabled through standard Telnet option negotiation. The sender of IAC WILL BM may define mappings from a single byte to a longer string. The receiver can accept or refuse a definition, and the sender must wait for that answer before using or redefining the macro byte.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides first negotiate the option. The sender then offers a byte-to-string mapping and waits for the receiver to accept or refuse it.

sections.title: Expanding a Macro Byte
sections.content: After a definition is accepted, the receiver behaves as though it received the expansion string whenever it receives the macro byte outside a BM subcommand. Expansion strings are not reinterpreted, so macro definitions cannot recursively expand. The IAC byte, decimal 255, cannot be defined as a macro byte.
sections.plainLanguage: An accepted macro byte stands for its longer expansion string. The expansion is not processed again as another macro, and IAC cannot be a macro byte.
